narrative.about: The yield on 10-year US Treasury notes, the benchmark for mortgages and long-term borrowing.

messages.rising: A rising 10-year yield usually reflects stronger growth or inflation expectations, or heavier Treasury supply, and it raises borrowing costs across the economy.
messages.falling: A falling 10-year yield usually reflects slower growth or inflation expectations, or demand for safe assets.
messages.steady: Long-term rate expectations are holding steady.

narrative.about: The yield on 2-year Treasury notes, the most sensitive to expected Federal Reserve policy.

messages.rising: A rising 2-year yield usually means markets expect the Fed to keep rates higher or raise them.
messages.falling: A falling 2-year yield usually means markets expect Fed rate cuts.
messages.steady: Expectations for Fed policy are holding steady.

narrative.about: The yield on 30-year Treasury bonds, the longest-dated benchmark.

messages.rising: A rising 30-year yield can reflect long-run inflation concerns or a higher premium for holding long-dated debt.
messages.falling: A falling 30-year yield can reflect lower long-run inflation expectations or demand for long-dated safe assets.
messages.steady: Long-run rate expectations are holding steady.

narrative.about: The yield on 5-year Treasury notes, a read on the medium-term rate and inflation outlook.

messages.rising: A rising 5-year yield usually reflects expectations of higher rates or inflation over the next few years.
messages.falling: A falling 5-year yield usually reflects expectations of lower rates or slower growth over the next few years.
messages.steady: Medium-term rate expectations are holding steady.

narrative.about: The effective yield on the ICE BofA US High Yield index: what below-investment-grade companies pay to borrow.

messages.rising: Rising high-yield borrowing costs can point to credit stress, or to higher rates feeding through to weaker companies.
messages.falling: Falling high-yield borrowing costs usually point to easy credit conditions and strong risk appetite.
messages.steady: Borrowing costs for weaker companies are holding steady.

messages.positive: A positive slope is the normal shape: investors are paid more to lend for longer, usually alongside expectations of growth.
messages.flat: A flat curve often appears late in an economic cycle or around turning points in Fed policy.
messages.inverted: An inverted 10-2 curve has come before most US recessions since the 1970s, though the lag has varied widely and it is not a timing tool.

messages.positive: A positive slope means longer money costs more, the usual pattern when growth and inflation are expected to hold up.
messages.flat: A flat middle of the curve suggests markets see little difference between the medium- and long-term outlook.
messages.inverted: An inversion here suggests markets expect rates to be lower in the long run than over the next five years, often a sign of expected slowdown.

messages.positive: A positive long end means investors want extra yield to hold the longest bonds, often tied to inflation or government-debt supply concerns.
messages.flat: A flat long end suggests investors see little extra risk in lending for 30 years rather than 10.
messages.inverted: An inverted long end is rare and usually reflects strong demand for the longest bonds, such as from pension funds, or deep pessimism about long-run growth.

messages.positive: A positive slope at the short end usually means markets expect rates to hold or rise over the next few years.
messages.flat: A flat short end often appears when markets expect the Fed to be near the end of a hiking or cutting cycle.
messages.inverted: An inverted short end usually means markets expect the Fed to cut rates within the next few years.

narrative.about: The high-yield index's effective yield minus the 10-year Treasury yield: a rough measure of the extra pay investors demand for credit risk.

extremes.high: an unusually wide spread, pricing elevated default risk
extremes.low: an unusually tight spread, with little extra pay for credit risk

messages.rising: A widening spread means investors want more compensation for default risk, often a risk-off signal.
messages.falling: A narrowing spread means investors are comfortable taking credit risk, usually a risk-on signal.
messages.steady: Appetite for credit risk is little changed.

narrative.about: Consumer prices compared with a year earlier (CPI, all urban consumers).

bands.text: Inflation is below the Fed's 2% goal, which gives it room to ease.
Inflation is close to the Fed's 2% goal.
Inflation is above the Fed's 2% goal, which keeps pressure on the Fed to hold rates up.

messages.rising: It has picked up over the last three months.
messages.falling: It has eased over the last three months.

narrative.about: The share of the labor force out of work and looking for a job.

messages.rising: A rising unemployment rate points to a cooling labor market.
messages.falling: A falling unemployment rate points to a tightening labor market, which can add to wage and inflation pressure.
messages.steady: The labor market is holding steady.

riseFromLow.text: The rate is {rise}pp above its 12-month low; rises of half a point or more have often come with recessions.

narrative.about: Total nonfarm payroll jobs compared with a year earlier.

bands.text: Payrolls are shrinking year over year, which has historically happened mainly in recessions.
Job growth under about 1% a year is slow by historical standards.
Job growth is running at a solid pace.

messages.rising: Growth has picked up over the last three months.
messages.falling: Growth has slowed over the last three months.
